chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 68 — Michael and Raphael Lament the Angels’ Judgment
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest complete primary-language text responsibly available for this chapter. No extant Aramaic or Greek wording has been identified for this Noahic unit within the Parables. The complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann's 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, is the translation base for all five verses: Enoch's written transmission of hidden things and parables, Michael's grief before Raphael over the angelic sentence, and the declaration that the rebels alone receive their everlasting portion because they acted as though they were the Lord. The chapter's shift from written inheritance to heavenly lament is retained without expansion. No unattested wording was supplied, and no modern English translation was used as the translation base.

verses.text: After this my grandfather Enoch gave me in a book the sign of all the hidden things, the parables that had been given to him, and he gathered them for me in the words of the book of parables.
verses.study: Noah receives revelation as a written inheritance. Signs, hidden things and parables are gathered into words so that the vision can outlast the seer's immediate presence.
crossReferences: Habakkuk 2:2 — revelation is written plainly for future witness
Revelation 1:11 — a vision is committed to a book for others

verses.text: On that day holy Michael answered Raphael, saying, ‘The power of the spirit carries me away and makes me tremble because of the severity of the judgment.’
verses.study: Michael is not emotionally untouched by the sentence. Heavenly fidelity includes trembling before the terrible weight of righteous judgment.
crossReferences: Habakkuk 3:16 — the prophet trembles at the coming day of distress
Revelation 8:1 — even heaven falls silent before unfolding judgment

verses.text: ‘Who can endure the severity of the judgment that has been carried out and remains?’
verses.study: The question emphasizes both what has begun and what continues. The angelic judgment is not a momentary shock but an abiding sentence difficult even to contemplate.
crossReferences: Psalm 76:7 — who can stand before God when His anger rises
Malachi 3:2 — who can endure the day of the Lord's coming

verses.text: Holy Michael answered again and said to Raphael, ‘Whose heart would not be softened by it, and whose inward parts would not be disturbed by this word of judgment that has gone out against those who were expelled in this way?’
verses.study: Compassionate disturbance does not deny justice. Michael's softened heart responds to the enormity of a judgment brought upon beings who chose expulsion through rebellion.
crossReferences: Jeremiah 4:19 — inward anguish responds to announced disaster
Luke 19:41–44 — judgment can be proclaimed with grief over those who refused peace

verses.text: When he stood before the Lord of Spirits, holy Michael said to Raphael, ‘They will not be accepted before the eye of the Lord, for the Lord of Spirits is angry with them because they acted as though they were the Lord. Therefore a hidden judgment will come upon them forever and ever. Neither angel nor human will receive their portion; they alone have received their judgment forever and ever.’
verses.study: The rebels' decisive offense is usurped lordship. Their portion is not imposed on other creatures: it belongs to those who uniquely chose this imitation of divine authority.
crossReferences: Isaiah 14:13–15 — self-exaltation toward divine status ends in descent
Jude 6 — angels who abandon their place are kept for lasting judgment
2 Peter 2:4 — sinning angels are reserved for judgment

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 68 begins with transmission. Enoch gathers signs, hidden things and parables into a book for Noah, making received revelation a trust passed between generations.
The scene then moves to Michael and Raphael. Michael trembles and grieves over the severity of judgment, showing that heavenly obedience does not require emotional indifference.

The angels' sentence is tied to attempted usurpation: they acted as though they were the Lord. The punishment corresponds to a rebellion that distorted delegated heavenly power into self-made lordship.
The chapter distinguishes compassion from reversal. Michael's heart is softened, yet the rebels alone receive the lasting portion their own transgression produced.

crossReferences: Jude 6 — rebellious angels kept for judgment
